title: Basic Nursing Care — Perioperative & Pre/Post-Procedure Care Basics (Set 14)
subtitle: Preoperative preparation and checklist, pre-op teaching (deep breathing, coughing, leg exercises, early ambulation), NPO/aspiration rationale, post-anesthesia airway and monitoring priorities, positioning, complication prevention (atelectasis, DVT), wound/dressing and pain observation, and reporting within scope
scenario: Assisting with care before and after a surgery or procedure: preparing the client, reinforcing pre-op teaching, keeping the recovering client safe (airway, positioning, safety), watching for complications, and reporting to the nurse—while procedures and consent remain with licensed staff.

steps.q: The overall purpose of preoperative preparation is to:

opts.text: Prepare the client physically and psychologically and ensure ordered pre-op steps are completed
opts.rat: Good pre-op care readies the client's body and mind and confirms that required preparations and orders are carried out for a safe procedure.

opts.text: Rush the client to surgery without any preparation
opts.rat: Skipping preparation increases risk; pre-op steps are important for safety.

opts.text: Hide all information from the client
opts.rat: Appropriate teaching and reassurance are part of pre-op care.

opts.text: Complete billing before anything else
opts.rat: Clinical preparation and safety, not billing, are the focus of pre-op care.

steps.q: Why is a client kept NPO (nothing by mouth) before surgery with anesthesia?

opts.text: To reduce the risk of aspiration (stomach contents entering the lungs) during anesthesia
opts.rat: An empty stomach lowers the chance of vomiting and aspirating during anesthesia, a serious complication.

opts.text: To punish the client
opts.rat: NPO is a safety measure, never punishment.

opts.text: Because food has no effect on anesthesia safety
opts.rat: Food in the stomach raises aspiration risk under anesthesia.

opts.text: To save money on meals
opts.rat: NPO is for aspiration prevention, not cost.

steps.q: Confirming that informed consent for the surgery has been obtained is:

opts.text: Verified as present on the chart before the procedure, with the consent itself obtained by the provider performing it
opts.rat: The technician can confirm the signed consent is in place, but obtaining informed consent is the responsibility of the provider doing the procedure.

opts.text: Obtained independently by the technician
opts.rat: Obtaining informed consent for a procedure is the provider's responsibility, not the technician's.

opts.text: Unnecessary for surgery
opts.rat: Informed consent is required before a surgical procedure.

opts.text: Something to skip if the unit is busy
opts.rat: Consent verification is essential and not skipped.

steps.q: A typical preoperative checklist item the technician may help with is:

opts.text: Ensuring the ID band is on and removing items like jewelry and dentures per policy
opts.rat: Confirming identification and removing jewelry, dentures, and similar items (per policy) are standard pre-op safety steps.

opts.text: Leaving all jewelry and dentures in place for surgery
opts.rat: These are typically removed before surgery for safety per policy.

opts.text: Removing the client's ID band
opts.rat: The ID band is kept on to verify identity, not removed.

opts.text: Feeding the client a large meal just before surgery
opts.rat: The client is NPO before surgery, not fed a large meal.

steps.q: Pre-op teaching often includes showing the client how to deep-breathe, cough, and do leg exercises because these help:

opts.text: Prevent post-operative complications such as lung problems and blood clots
opts.rat: Deep breathing/coughing help prevent atelectasis and pneumonia, and leg exercises/early movement help prevent blood clots after surgery.

opts.text: Make the surgery take longer
opts.rat: These measures aid recovery; they do not affect surgery length.

opts.text: Replace the need for the surgery
opts.rat: They support recovery, not replace the procedure.

opts.text: Have no effect on recovery
opts.rat: They meaningfully reduce common post-op complications.

steps.q: A client is visibly anxious before surgery and has questions. The technician should:

opts.text: Provide reassurance, allow the client to express concerns, and notify the nurse of questions needing answers
opts.rat: Emotional support and routing clinical questions to the nurse address the client's psychological preparation appropriately.

opts.text: Tell the client their feelings do not matter
opts.rat: Dismissing feelings is nontherapeutic; support is part of pre-op care.

opts.text: Ignore the client's questions entirely
opts.rat: Questions are acknowledged and routed to the nurse as needed.

opts.text: Give detailed medical answers beyond their scope
opts.rat: Clinical questions beyond scope are referred to the nurse or provider.

steps.q: Obtaining baseline vital signs before surgery is important because they:

opts.text: Provide a comparison point to help detect changes after the procedure
opts.rat: Baseline vitals let the team recognize post-op changes that may signal a problem.

opts.text: Are never needed for surgery
opts.rat: Baseline vitals are a standard, important part of pre-op assessment.

opts.text: Only matter for billing
opts.rat: They are clinically important for detecting change, not administrative.

opts.text: Should be skipped to save time
opts.rat: Baseline vitals are obtained, not skipped.

steps.q: Immediately after anesthesia, the HIGHEST priority in monitoring the recovering client is:

opts.text: Airway and breathing, along with level of consciousness and vital signs
opts.rat: After anesthesia, protecting the airway and ensuring adequate breathing are the top priorities, with close monitoring of consciousness and vitals.

opts.text: Whether the client's TV is working
opts.rat: Comfort items are minor compared with airway and breathing.

opts.text: The client's meal preferences
opts.rat: Meal preferences are not the immediate post-anesthesia priority.

opts.text: The color of the client's gown
opts.rat: This is irrelevant to post-anesthesia safety.

steps.q: A client who is still drowsy and not fully awake after anesthesia is best positioned:

opts.text: On their side (or as ordered) to help keep the airway clear and reduce aspiration risk
opts.rat: Side-lying helps secretions or vomit drain away and protects the airway in a client who is not fully alert.

opts.text: Flat on the back and left unmonitored
opts.rat: A not-fully-awake client on their back is at aspiration risk and needs monitoring; side-lying is safer.

opts.text: Sitting fully upright and made to walk immediately
opts.rat: A drowsy post-anesthesia client is at fall risk; immediate walking is unsafe.

opts.text: Face-down with the face pressed into the pillow
opts.rat: This can obstruct the airway and is unsafe.

steps.q: Which post-operative finding should the technician report to the nurse promptly?

opts.text: Increasing bleeding, a drop or change in vital signs, decreasing responsiveness, or difficulty breathing
opts.rat: These can indicate serious post-op complications (hemorrhage, shock, respiratory or neurological problems) requiring immediate attention.

opts.text: The client resting comfortably with stable vitals
opts.rat: This is reassuring, not a concern to report urgently.

opts.text: A clean, dry, intact dressing
opts.rat: An intact dressing is an expected, normal finding.

opts.text: The client asking for a blanket
opts.rat: A routine comfort request is not a complication.

steps.q: To help prevent lung complications (such as atelectasis) after surgery, the technician should encourage the client to:

opts.text: Deep-breathe and cough regularly and use the incentive spirometer as taught
opts.rat: Regular deep breathing, coughing, and incentive spirometry re-expand the lungs and help prevent post-op atelectasis and pneumonia.

opts.text: Lie still and breathe as shallowly as possible
opts.rat: Shallow breathing and immobility promote atelectasis.

opts.text: Avoid all movement for several days
opts.rat: Prolonged immobility increases complications; movement and breathing exercises help.

opts.text: Hold the breath as long as possible repeatedly
opts.rat: This is not the recommended technique; deep breathing and spirometry are.

steps.q: To help prevent blood clots (such as deep vein thrombosis) after surgery, a helpful measure is:

opts.text: Encouraging early movement/ambulation and leg exercises as ordered
opts.rat: Movement and leg exercises promote circulation and help prevent clots from forming during post-op recovery.

opts.text: Keeping the client completely immobile for as long as possible
opts.rat: Immobility increases clot risk; movement helps prevent it.

opts.text: Massaging the legs vigorously to break up any clots
opts.rat: Vigorously massaging the legs is unsafe and could dislodge a clot; it is not done.

opts.text: Restricting all leg motion indefinitely
opts.rat: Restricting motion raises clot risk; gentle activity is encouraged as ordered.

steps.q: When observing a post-operative surgical dressing, the technician should:

opts.text: Check for bleeding or increasing drainage and report changes, without removing the initial dressing unless directed
opts.rat: Monitoring the dressing for bleeding/drainage and reporting changes is within scope; the first surgical dressing is usually changed by licensed staff or per order.

opts.text: Remove the surgical dressing to look at the incision out of curiosity
opts.rat: The initial dressing is not removed casually; doing so risks contamination and bleeding.

opts.text: Ignore any drainage that appears
opts.rat: Drainage changes are observed and reported, not ignored.

opts.text: Reinforce the dressing and never tell anyone
opts.rat: Changes are reported to the nurse, not concealed.

steps.q: Regarding post-operative pain, the technician should:

opts.text: Ask about and observe for pain, provide comfort measures within scope, and report it to the nurse for management
opts.rat: Recognizing and reporting pain and offering comfort measures support the client while the nurse manages medication and treatment.

opts.text: Assume post-op clients never have pain
opts.rat: Post-op pain is common and should be assessed and reported.

opts.text: Tell the client to simply ignore the pain
opts.rat: Dismissing pain is nontherapeutic; it is reported for management.

opts.text: Independently administer additional pain medication
opts.rat: Medication administration follows orders and scope; pain is reported to the nurse.

steps.q: A post-operative client becomes nauseated and begins to vomit. The technician should FIRST:

opts.text: Position the client to protect the airway (such as turning the head or side-lying) and report to the nurse
opts.rat: Protecting the airway prevents aspiration during vomiting; reporting allows treatment of the nausea.

opts.text: Lay the drowsy client flat on their back and leave
opts.rat: Flat positioning during vomiting risks aspiration, especially if the client is drowsy.

opts.text: Give the client a large drink of water immediately
opts.rat: Giving fluids during active vomiting can worsen aspiration risk.

opts.text: Ignore it and continue other tasks
opts.rat: Vomiting post-op requires airway protection and reporting, not ignoring.

steps.q: Monitoring urinary output after surgery is important because:

opts.text: Inability to void or low output can signal a problem and should be reported
opts.rat: Post-op clients may have difficulty voiding; tracking output and reporting problems supports timely intervention.

opts.text: Urinary output has no relevance after surgery
opts.rat: Output is an important indicator of recovery and fluid status.

opts.text: Output is only tracked before surgery
opts.rat: Post-op output is monitored as part of recovery.

opts.text: The client should be discouraged from voiding
opts.rat: Voiding is encouraged as able; inability to void is reported.

steps.q: Because a client recovering from anesthesia may be drowsy or unsteady, the technician should:

opts.text: Take fall-prevention measures—assist with movement and use safety measures per policy
opts.rat: Post-anesthesia drowsiness and dizziness increase fall risk, so assistance and safety measures protect the client.

opts.text: Let the client get up and walk alone right away
opts.rat: Unassisted early ambulation after anesthesia risks falls.

opts.text: Assume the client is steady and needs no help
opts.rat: Recovering clients are often unsteady and need assistance.

opts.text: Leave the drowsy client unmonitored on a high surface
opts.rat: This is unsafe; monitoring and fall precautions are needed.

steps.q: To reduce infection risk in a post-operative client, the technician should:

opts.text: Perform hand hygiene and follow wound-care and precaution orders
opts.rat: Hand hygiene and following ordered wound-care/precautions are key to preventing surgical-site and other infections.

opts.text: Skip hand hygiene to save time
opts.rat: Hand hygiene is essential to infection prevention.

opts.text: Touch the wound with bare, unwashed hands
opts.rat: This introduces infection risk and violates infection-control principles.

opts.text: Ignore ordered precautions
opts.rat: Ordered precautions are followed to protect the client.

steps.q: Which is an early sign the technician should report as a possible post-operative complication?

opts.text: A rising pulse with a falling blood pressure and increasing restlessness
opts.rat: These together can indicate developing bleeding or shock after surgery and require prompt reporting.

opts.text: Stable vital signs and a comfortable, alert client
opts.rat: These are reassuring, expected findings.

opts.text: The client sipping ordered fluids without difficulty
opts.rat: Tolerating ordered fluids is a good sign, not a complication.

opts.text: The client dozing comfortably with normal breathing
opts.rat: Comfortable rest with normal breathing is reassuring.

steps.q: Overall, the technician's role in perioperative care is to:

opts.text: Assist with preparation, support the client, monitor and provide basic care, watch for complications, and report—while procedures, consent, and medical management belong to licensed staff
opts.rat: The technician prepares, supports, monitors, and reports within scope, while surgery, consent, and clinical management are handled by licensed providers and nurses.

opts.text: Perform the surgical procedure
opts.rat: Performing procedures is far outside the technician's scope.

opts.text: Obtain surgical informed consent independently
opts.rat: Consent for a procedure is obtained by the provider performing it.

opts.text: Manage anesthesia and prescribe medications
opts.rat: Anesthesia and prescribing are outside the technician's scope.

reference: Aligned to the California BVNPT Psychiatric Technician exam content area: Basic Nursing Care (perioperative and pre/post-procedure care). Written from standard psychiatric-technician and nursing references at an introductory level. Concepts are stated conceptually and marked for faculty confirmation: pre-op preparation and checklist (ID band, removing jewelry/dentures per policy), NPO/aspiration rationale, verifying (not obtaining) consent, pre-op teaching (deep breathing, coughing, leg exercises, early ambulation), baseline vitals; and post-anesthesia priorities (airway/breathing/consciousness), side-lying positioning for the not-fully-awake client, complication recognition (bleeding/shock, respiratory), atelectasis and DVT prevention, dressing/pain/nausea/output monitoring, infection prevention, and fall precautions. Roles reflect the technician's scope: assist, support, monitor, and report, while procedures, consent, anesthesia, and prescribing belong to licensed staff. No specific NPO durations, vital-sign values, or medication details are asserted. Builds on NPO (bnc-core-05), incentive spirometry (bnc-core-09), ambulation/gait belt (bnc-core-07), and procedure prep/consent (bnc-core-13). Pending faculty review.
